Row.english: Galeni's Legitimacy

My liege, we are a seperatist state. We may have won our independence on the battlefield, but the Boruvian Empire still lays claim to our lands. Worse, the Valegorn Palatinate has not yet recognized our legitimacy. This means that the Empire can annex our capital without diplomatic reprisal. To counter this, our diplomats are working hard to gain full legitimacy and put an end to the Boruvian claim.
Row.german: Herr, wir sind ein separatistischer Staat. Wir haben zwar unsere Unabhängigkeit auf dem Schlachtfeld erworben, dennoch erhebt das Boruvian Empire noch immer Anspruch auf unser Land. Schlimmer, das Valegorn Palatinat hat unsere Legitimität noch nicht anerkannt, folglich kann das Empire unsere Hauptstadt ohne diplomatische Repressalie annektieren. Dem entgegenzuwirken, arbeiten unsere Diplomaten intensivst daran, volle Legitimität zu erreichen, um den boruvianischen Anspruch zu beenden.

Row.english: My liege, I am come to inform you, we have achieved some measure of sympathy in the Palatinate's court. Through our piety and knightly orders, there are some in the Valegorn Palatinate who speak well of us and advance our cause. Hold the line, and we will continue to pursue legitimacy.
Row.german: Herr, ich komme Euch zu berichten, daß wir vor dem Gericht des Palatinats einen Schritt vorwärts gekommen sind. Unserer Pietät und Ritterorden ist es geschuldet, daß uns einige im Valegorn Palatinat wohl gesinnt sind. Mit Geduld werden wir die Angelegenheit unserer Legitimität weiter verfolgen.

Row.english: More and more in Valegorn champion our cause. We continue to court Valegorn's sympathies. Stay firm. The Empire may still be strong, but her star is fading.
Row.german: Es werden stets mehr in Valegorn, die unsere Sache verfechten. Wir werden weiterhin um Valegorns Sympathien werben. Zwar ist das Empire noch mächtig, doch sein Stern ist am verblassen.

Row.english: The court of the Valegorn Palatitate is in full debate. It is not yet certain whether they will judge for Boruvia or for Galeni. But one thing is certain: you have shaken the foundations of Imperial rule. We are very close now.
Row.german: Valegorns Gerichtshof befindet sich in umfassender Debatte. Noch ist es nicht sicher, ob für Boruvia oder Galena gestimmt werden wird; eines jedoch ist klar, durch Euch wurde das Empire in seinen Grundfesten erschüttert. Wir sind der Entscheidung nahe.

Row.english: A diplomatic coup! We have proven to the world that Galeni stands on its own as a power to be reckoned with. The Imperials have tucked their tails and ended their claim to Maltessa! We have gained legitimacy!
Row.german: Ein diplomatischer Staatsstreich! Wir haben der Welt Galenis Stärke bewiesen. Die kaiserlichen Hoheiten zogen ihren Schwanz ein und beendeten ihren Anspruch auf Maltessa! Wir erwarben Legitimität!

Row.english: Your Excellency, we may seize Galeni’s and Berany’s Capitols without diplomatic reprisal. Such is our legitimate claim to our traditional lands against the separatists. However, it should be noted that the Galenite knightly orders have aroused interest in Valegorn’s court. This is cause of mild alarm.
Row.german: Mein Fürst, es mag uns gelingen Galenis und Beranys Hauptstädte ohne diplomatische Vergeltung zu beschlagnahmen. Das ist unser legitimer Anspruch auf unser traditionelles Land entgegen der Separaristen. Allerdings sollte bedacht werden, daß Galenis Ritterorden am Valegorn Gerichtshof Wohlwollen fand. Ein Anlass zur Besorgnis.

Row.english: Your Excellency, Galeni’s knightly orders continue to flourish, and Valegorn continues to warm toward these upstarts. If this trend is not reversed, our rightful claim against Galeni may one day be revoked.
Row.german: Mein Fürst, weiterhin florieren Galenis Ritterorden und Valegorn erwärmt sich zunehmend für diese Emporkömmlinge. Wird diese Tendenz nicht umgekehrt, könnte unser rechtmäßiger Anspruch gegen Galeni eines Tages widerrufen werden.

Row.english: Your Excellency, our rightful claim against Maltessa is in growing jeopardy. There are those within the Valegorn Palatinate now suggesting that Galeni be granted full rights. Should this trend continue, we will not be in a position to crush the separatists.
Row.german: Mein Fürst, unser rechtmäßiger Anspruch auf Maltessa ist in wachsender Gefahr. Innerhalb des Valegorn Palinats sprechen sich einige dafür aus, Galeni volle Rechte einzuräumen. Falls diese Tendenz anhält, werden wir nicht in der Lage sein, die Separatisten zu zerschlagen.

Row.english: Your Excellency, a hot debate is now in progress within the court of Valegorn as to whether to grant Galeni full independent rights. If you wish to annex Maltessa and destroy the separatists, the time is now or never.
Row.german: Exzellenz, innerhalb des Valegorn Gerichtshofs findet jetzt eine heiße Debatte statt, ob Galeni volle selbstständige Rechte eingeräumt werden sollen. Die Zeit ist jetzt oder nie, wolltet Ihr Maltessa annektieren und die Separatisten vernichten.

Row.english: Your Excellency, I regret to inform you that the Valegorn Palatinate has issued full legitimacy to Galeni. They are to be recognized with full rights as a Realm. Our claim to Maltessa is forfeit. Fortunately, we may still move against Beran, as no such diplomatic favor has yet been extended to Berany.
Row.german: Exzellenz, ich bedaure Euch mitteilen zu müssen, daß daß dasValegorn Palatinat Galeni volle Legitimität ausgestellt hat. Als Reich hat es volle Rechtezu genießen. Unser Anspruch auf Maltessa ist verwirkt. Erfreulicherweise können wir noch gegen Beran vorgehen, da solcherart Gefälligkeiten noch nicht auf Berany ausgedehnt wurden.

Row.english: An interesting development in the south and east. Galeni, recently formed from a band of upstarts and adventurers, has gained some noteworthy mention. Knightly orders have risen. If the trend continues, their strategy may succeed in gaining attention of the Valegorn Palatinate. It is too soon to breathe the word, 'legitimacy,' but 'noteworthy mention' is in the wind.
Row.german: Interessante Entwicklung im Süden, wie Osten: Galeni, das noch vor kurzem eine Bande Emporkömmlinge und Abenteuerer war, hat sich bemerkenswerte Notiz erworben. Ritterorden haben sich gebildet. Falls diese Tendenz anhält, mag diese Strategie die Aufmerksamkeit des Valegorn Palatinats gewinnen. Bald wird es ‘Legitimität’ hauchen, doch “Erwähnenswert” hängt in der Luft.

Row.english: Galeni continues to makes diplomatic strides with the Valegorn Palatinate, while the Boruvian claim to Maltessa becomes ever more shrill. If the Boruvians have an Emperor worthy of the throne, they will decide this matter on the battlefield before Galeni reaches legitimacy.
Row.german: Galeni macht in Bezug auf das Valegorn Palatinat weiterhin beachtliche diplomatische Fortschritte, indes der boruvianische Anspruch auf Maltessa immer hysterischer wird. Sollten die Boruvianer einen Kaiser würdig seines Thrones haben, werden sie diese Sache auf dem Schlachtfeld entscheiden, bevor Galeni Legitimität erreicht.

Row.english: A terrible debate has ensued within the Valegorn Palatinate. It will decide the legitimacy of Galeni. The Boruvian claim is fast slipping away.
Row.german: Eine erschreckende Debatte vollzog sich innerhalb des Valegorn Palatinats. Es wird die Entscheidung der Legitimität Galenis treffen. Der boruvianische Anspruch schwindet zusehens.

Row.english: We bring news, my liege. Galeni has gained legitimacy. The Boruvian Empire has officially forfeited her claim to Maltessa.
Row.german: Wir bringen Kunde, Herr. Galeni erwarb seine Legitimität. Das Boruvian Empire hat offiziell seinen Anspruch auf Maltessa verwirkt.

Row.english: My liege, the envoys of Sonneneve and Sirucil have both approached us and demanded that we declare support for one of them.\n\nOur people are fed up with isolation, and they are hungry for revenge on the humans who destroy our forests - we have no choice but to agree to join with our brothers in Sirucil - the forests will soon be filled with the blood of our enemies.
Row.german: Herr, Sonneneves und Sirucils Gesandte kamen auf uns mit der Forderung zu, unsere Unterstützung für einen von ihnen zu erklären.\n\nUnser Volk ist seiner Isolation müde und dürstet nach Rache gegen die Menschen, die unsere Wälder vernichten. Wir haben keine andere Wahl, als uns mit unserern Brüdern in Sirucil zu verbinden. Bald werden die Wälder vom Blut unserer Feide triefen.

Row.english: My liege, the envoys of Sonneneve and Sirucil have both approached us and demanded that we declare support for one of them.\n\nOur people are eager for us to attempt reconciliation with the humans of this world, and so we must choose to side with Soneeneve - together with our High Elf brothers we shall bring peace to the world through diplomacy.
Row.german: Herr, Sonneneves und Sirucils Gesandte kamen auf uns mit der Forderung zu, unsere Unterstützung für einen von ihnen zu erklären.\n\nUnser Volk begehrt Aussöhnung mit den Menschen dieser Welt, somit haben wir uns auf die Seite Sonneneves zu schlagen. Zusammen mit unseren Brüdern, der Hohen Elfen, wollen wir anhand Diplomatie Frieden erreichen.

Longbowmen arrive with waxed bowstrings; by evening even lazy officers know where Ariselle has placed its trust. They are ordinary enough until orders harden them into a weapon.
In Ariselle, Druids are not praised for elegance. They are kept because bow-work must be done when banners and speeches have failed.
Ask a veteran what Dragoon are worth and he will point to the part of the map nobody wants to enter. When the charge begins, neat plans become dust, hooves and screaming geometry.
There are always traces of hammer marks on fresh timber around Siege Tower. Recruits notice them first; survivors learn the day has become serious.
Ariselle's musters list them as siege crews. Camp followers use shorter names, usually spoken after counting the wounded.
Nobody writes songs for Ship of the Line unless the battle goes very badly. Their trade is practical, close, and remembered in scars.
A commander buys Spearmen for one reason and later discovers three more. A wall of points is their argument, and cavalry usually understands it too late.
Where Calland sends Footmen, villages shut doors early and quartermasters begin arguing over extra pay.
The first sign of Greenford Skirmishers is often not a banner but chalk marks on doors. After that, the careful men look for cover.
Slingers keep their own habits: charms, knives, lucky straps, bad wine. Superstition is cheaper than armor and easier to carry.
The manuals call them mounted troops; the troops call them useful, dangerous, cursed, or late, depending on who survived the march.
Few recruits dream of joining Siege Tower. Most arrive by debt, duty, pride, or a captain who lied convincingly at the tavern.
Bereska keeps Halberdiers ready for work that polite courtiers prefer not to describe too closely. dragonslayer marks their methods.
Around the cookfires, Saboteur are judged by small things: dry powder, sharp edges, quiet feet, and whether they panic first.
An enemy who sees Rangers clearly has already been allowed too close. Their better stories start earlier and end elsewhere.
Paymasters hate them, officers need them, and common soldiers make room when Bereskan Crossbows come through camp with quiet wagers over distance.
The badge of Druids changes from realm to realm; the look in their eyes stays much the same before ugly work begins.
Some troops win ground by courage. Ballista prefer timing, pressure, and the old military art of making another man regret standing there.
Odenheim sends Spearmen where discipline must look like confidence. The difference is usually invisible until the first retreat.
A province can sleep through many dangers, but not Shaman. Even rumors of them put smiths, priests and debtors to work.
Slingers are expensive in ways not always written on the ledger: fodder, repairs, apologies, graves, and favors owed afterward.
When Eagles drill, the rhythm is plain enough. When they fight, the same rhythm becomes accusation, answer, and sentence.
The old hands among Mountain Ponies have few heroic poses. They check straps, curse weather, and listen for the silence before orders.
In tavern talk, Levies become larger than life. In battle they are worse: smaller, nearer, and much harder to bargain with.
Give Legionnaire bad ground and they complain. Give them useful ground and the enemy complains louder. They are ordinary enough until orders harden them into a weapon.
No marshal trusts Provocateur completely; no marshal likes marching without them. That is how many necessary things enter an army.
Bowmen carry arrows bundled in oilcloth and the tired pride of troops who know exactly how little mercy the campaign has budgeted.
A neat line on the roster hides the truth: Trebuchet are arguments made of people, gear, fear, and a little professional spite.
Children run beside Men-at-Arms on parade days. Soldiers watch their hands instead, because parade habits rarely survive contact.
The road behind Chariots is easy to recognize: trampled grass, worried locals, and officers pretending this was the plan.
Evengaad's enemies have several names for Engineers. None are flattering; most are accurate enough to be repeated quietly.
If Trebuchet have a virtue, it is not kindness. It is the stubborn capacity to make bad orders slightly less fatal.
The best of Merfolk know when to hold, when to move, and when an officer's confidence is just fear wearing a polished belt.
Every army has troops like Water Elemental: complained about in peace, searched for in crisis, and blamed by survivors afterward.
Axemen do not need legends. They need rations, repair, room to work, and an enemy who has misunderstood the distance.
Some units bring courage to a field. Darkwood Wraith bring method, which is colder, slower, and often more useful.
The smell of chalk marks on doors follows Hunters long after they pass. In frightened villages, that is enough to start rumors.

The first sign of Treant is often not a banner but creaking winches. After that, the careful men look for cover.
Renegade Fusiliers keep their own habits: charms, knives, lucky straps, bad wine. Superstition is cheaper than armor and easier to carry.
The manuals call them irregulars; the troops call them useful, dangerous, cursed, or late, depending on who survived the march, as Cragenwaste records it.
Few recruits dream of joining Crossbows. Most arrive by debt, duty, pride, or a captain who lied convincingly at the tavern.
Cragenwaste keeps Mastodons ready for work that polite courtiers prefer not to describe too closely. Give them a door, a beast, or a proud formation; they prefer things that break loudly.
Around the cookfires, Mogen Minelayers are judged by small things: dry powder, sharp edges, quiet feet, and whether they panic first.
An enemy who sees Ballista clearly has already been allowed too close. Their better stories start earlier and end elsewhere.
Paymasters hate them, officers need them, and common soldiers make room when Rock Troll come through camp with campfires too close to the road.
The badge of Goblin Slaves changes from realm to realm; the look in their eyes stays much the same before ugly work begins.
Some troops win ground by courage. Orc Javelins prefer timing, pressure, and the old military art of making another man regret standing there.
Khazoth sends Abomination where discipline must look like confidence. The difference is usually invisible until the first retreat.
A province can sleep through many dangers, but not Old Betty. Even rumors of them put smiths, priests and debtors to work.
Siege Tower are expensive in ways not always written on the ledger: fodder, repairs, apologies, graves, and favors owed afterward.
When Tunnel Dwarves drill, the rhythm is plain enough. When they fight, the same rhythm becomes accusation, answer, and sentence.
The old hands among Heavy Guard have few heroic poses. They check straps, curse weather, and listen for the silence before orders.
In tavern talk, Heavy Crossbows become larger than life. In battle they are worse: smaller, nearer, and much harder to bargain with.
Give Clay Golem bad ground and they complain. Give them useful ground and the enemy complains louder. They stand where something valuable would otherwise be killed.
No marshal trusts Ballista completely; no marshal likes marching without them. That is how many necessary things enter an army.
Dryads carry false names at every inn and the tired pride of troops who know exactly how little mercy the campaign has budgeted.
A neat line on the roster hides the truth: Elven Longbows are arguments made of people, gear, fear, and a little professional spite.
Children run beside Spellbinder on parade days. Soldiers watch their hands instead, because parade habits rarely survive contact.
The road behind Eagle Lord is easy to recognize: trampled grass, worried locals, and officers pretending this was the plan.
Sonneneve's enemies have several names for Unicorn. None are flattering; most are accurate enough to be repeated quietly.
If Elven Riders have a virtue, it is not kindness. It is the stubborn capacity to make bad orders slightly less fatal.
The best of Treant know when to hold, when to move, and when an officer's confidence is just fear wearing a polished belt.
Every army has troops like Drowned of the Deep: complained about in peace, searched for in crisis, and blamed by survivors afterward.
Skeletons do not need legends. They need rations, repair, room to work, and an enemy who has misunderstood the distance.
Some units bring courage to a field. Bone Demon bring method, which is colder, slower, and often more useful.
The smell of chalk marks on doors follows Will o' Wisp long after they pass. In frightened villages, that is enough to start rumors.
A careless scout sees only Lich. A careful one counts tracks, listens for tools, and rides back faster than he came.

Against weak foes, Nightmare look ordinary. Against strong ones, their value becomes clear in the parts of the line still standing.
Their officers describe Mandrake with tidy words. The men facing them use older language: trouble, thunder, teeth, smoke.
A battlefield gives Folk Singer many materials to work with: panic, mud, pride, bad footing, and the moment before courage fails.

Scouts have learned one honest lesson: most battles are not decided by heroes, but by someone doing miserable work correctly.
